newsitem.title: CHINA: China vows crackdown on financial institutions.
newsitem.headline: China vows crackdown on financial institutions.

text.p: China's central bank governor Dai Xianglong on Thursday vowed to intensify a crackdown on irregularities among financial institutions to avoid a crisis similar to the one that has battered Thailand.

"To prevent financial risks...the central bank will further intensify supervision and regulation of financial institutions, ban financial institutions that were illegally set up and ban illegal financial activities," Dai told a news conference.
"We will investigate and punish operations that violate laws and regulations and prevent and crack down on financial crime," said the governor of the People's Bank of China.
Some financial institutions have reportedly been charging exorbitant interest rates or falsifying their accounts.

Among the worst cases was an urban credit cooperative in the booming southern province of Guangdong that was unable to meet demands when depositors tried to withdraw their money, Dai said without giving more details.
The central bank would streamline the country's thousands of small credit cooperatives, merging them into larger financial institutions or dissolving them, Dai said.
"We should overhaul urban credit cooperatives," he added.
Dai pledged loans to profitable credit cooperatives that faced temporary difficulties but said those that deliberately reneged on their loans would be forced through legal means to repay.
Preventing financial risk topped the central bank's priority list, he said when asked what measures China had taken to prevent a financial crisis similar to that in Thailand.
Thailand plunged into crisis last month when it floated the baht in what amounted to a currency devaluation for the once-tiger economy due to market pressure.
Financial risk could be lowered by improving the quality of credit, Dai said, adding that poor credit increased inflationary pressure.
Risk among state banks had been reduced since June when they were ordered to pull out of the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets as part of a clampdown on overheated stock trading, the governor said.
Chinese brokerages used to borrow heavily from banks through the bond repurchase markets on the stock markets for speculative equity investment.
China launched last June interbank state debt trading on a local currency interbank market, in which only banks that are members of the interbank market are allowed to conduct trading.
By the end of June, the combined assets of financial institutions stood at 13.28 trillion yuan ($1.6 billion), up 680 billion yuan from the beginning of the year, central bank statistics showed.
Assets of financial institutions rose by an annual average of 24.4 percent between 1990 and 1996, the figures showed.

Outstanding loans of financial institutions stood at 6.87 trillion yuan at the end of July, up 450.3 billion yuan from the beginning of the year but down 15.6 billion yuan compared with the same 1996 period, the statistics showed.

The amount of unpaid interest owed to state-owned banks on loans in arrears of up to two years totalled 143.1 billion yuan at the end of June, an increase of 24.6 billion yuan, or 20.76 percent, from the start of the year, the bank said.
